To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
diabetes causes a chronic and inappropriate activation in kidney epithelial cells of negative regulators of inflammation and immunity.

diabetes induces molecular signatures of tissue damage and chronic inflammation in the kidney, and that this is associated with the induction of negative regulatory responses that impair epithelial immunity and may contribute to increased susceptibility to infection.
chronic inflammation in diabetes mellitus leads to dysregulated immune responses and increased risk of infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular mechanisms of renal inflammation in diabetes and how this may affect the immune system.
the role of inflammation in diabetic nephropathy, and the mechanisms of inflammation-induced tissue damage.
the mechanisms of immune dysfunction in diabetes mellitus, which may have important implications in other inflammatory diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
diabetes mellitus is a chronic inflammatory disease of the kidney, and the kidney is the most important target organ of this disease.

chronic inflammation in diabetes mellitus is not only a consequence of tissue damage and metabolic abnormalities, but also a consequence of the immune system being unable to mount an effective response to infection and tissue damage.
the kidney in diabetes is in a state of chronic low-grade inflammation and impaired immunity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
diabetes-induced tissue damage triggers a series of events that lead to the activation of counter-regulating anti-inflammatory pathways.
diabetes mellitus is a state of impaired renal immunity, which may contribute to the increased risk of infections and progression of diabetic nephritis.
diabetes impairs renal epithelial immunity by triggering negative regulatory responses to inflammation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
diabetes impairs renal immunity and this contributes to renal infection, which may be one of the mechanisms that lead to progression of diabetic renal disease.
the immune system in diabetes is not just hyperactivated but is also hyper-regulated, leading to a state of immune deficiency.
the chronic inflammation that characterizes diabetes mellitus impairs renal immunity.
